sentence: The theremin was the most eye-catching element in the first concert of this festival, devoted to the Czech composer Bohuslav Martinu. The instrument was invented in 1920 and is played by manipulating an electromagnetic field with magician-like gestures, its hollow keening notes seemingly plucked from the air. On Friday at the Fisher Center in Annandale-on-Hudson, N.Y., it joined a cast of traditional instruments — oboe, piano, strings — in Martinu’s “Fantasia” from 1944, creating an unexpectedly moving amalgam of instrumental colors. The work captures something of the essence of this artist, who embraced both the turbulence and the technological marvels of the 20th century, and who delighted in unusual groupings of instruments that work their charm as much through choreography as sound.

sentence: This year marks both Botstein’s 50th year as president of Bard College and the 35th iteration of the festival, which he has built into a summer institution: two weekends of concerts, panel discussions, and lectures exploring the life and work of a single composer, accompanied by a scholarly volume of essays. The subject is as likely to be a household name as an overlooked figure, but the program always stretches beyond familiar repertoire. That mix of intellectual ambition and freedom from commercial pressures is rare in music-making in the United States, and it flourishes here. Judging by Friday’s stimulating opener, this year’s exploration of Martinu, a restless exile equally fluent in Czech folk song, Neo-Classicism and the hum of the modern world, invites audiences to discover one of the most distinct and delightful voices of his time.

sentence: Martinu was born in 1890 in a clock tower in the small Bohemian town of Policka, where his father was the fire watcher. Ninety-nine steps above ground, the family lived in a single square room with a commanding view of the countryside, a vantage point that may explain the composer’s signature blend of pastoral idyll with cool detachment. The lilting, off-kilter rhythms of nearby Moravia filtered into his music long after he traded his homeland for a life of exile.

sentence: The 1938 Munich Agreement, which ceded parts of his homeland to Nazi Germany, deeply embittered Martinu. His breathless Double Concerto for two string orchestras, piano and tympani reflects his political anguish during that time. Its performance by the Orchestra Now was a highlight of Friday’s program. The musicians were divided into two orchestras placed on either side of Botstein’s podium, with the pianist (the incisive Michael Stephen Brown) caught in the middle like an anxious go-between. From the first statement of the terse, propulsive theme, the music hurtled forward with Martinu’s trademark rhythmic drive, while the split-stage arrangement added visual drama, the two ensembles squaring off amid the rumbling drums of war.

sentence: The Double Concerto also points to Martinu’s interest in exploring group dynamics in his music. His output includes many variations on the concerto grosso, a Baroque form that gave collective soloists a more democratic role than the Romantic hero. In his works, small ensembles act as shifting alliances — forming, dissolving, and realigning — while negotiating their relationship with the larger body. That instinct was just as present in the “Fantasia,” in which the theremin’s uncanny whine (it was played with some audible jitters by Dorit Chrysler) haloed the more full-throated lyricism of the oboist Alexandra Knoll, the pianist Orion Weiss and the Balourdet Quartet.

sentence: As Botstein noted from the stage, there is little in this music that betrays anxiety. Yet behind that apparent ease, and the astonishing fluency with which Martinu produced work after work, was a restless, probing mind. An unpublished notebook by the composer recently found its way into Beckerman’s hands. In it, Martinu reflects on the question of sincerity in music: Can we ever be sure that what sounds heartfelt truly is? That kind of self-scrutiny, Beckerman said, reveals an artist skeptical of the tidy systems and manifestoes that dominated midcentury musical thought. Through decades of exile and in an age defined by ideological binaries, Martinu held fast to his own voice and to an intellectual independence that refused to be boxed in. “Yes, there is a mystery,” he wrote, “but no system will tell us what it is.”

sentence: Most progressives, historians or not, cringe at the slogan and believe it captures something vital and malevolent that drives Trump's words and policies. Jacksonian Democrats expanded the franchise to include nearly all white men but, at the same time, made it harder for free African Americans to vote. Labor unionists in the early twentieth century achieved higher wages for their members but demonized Chinese immigrants as servile "coolies" who, charged Samuel Gompers, never went on strike because they "haven't attained some degree of manhood and independence." Liberal Democratic politicians in the past century oversaw the building of a middle-class society, but Black people, Latinos, Asians, women, and homosexuals had to organize mass movements to claim their rightful place in it and convince many of those officeholders to support them.

sentence: Now, as before, progressives cannot be effective in calling for great changes in our society if they allow their adversaries to claim the mantle of patriotism for themselves alone. But neither she nor other progressives who eschew patriotism offer any convincing guidance about how to carry out their laudable objectives in a world in which nation-states reign supreme and likely will for decades to come. sentence: In certain contexts, chatbots and avatars could be useful tools for processing a death — particularly if they’re treated as spaces of reflection, like diaries. The uncanny verisimilitude of many of these avatars complicates that and makes it more likely that their ultimate result will not be helping people process grief, but rather allowing them a means of avoiding it.

sentence: I've talked on Techdirt about just a few of my AI-related experiments over the past few years, including how I use it  to help me edit pieces, which I still write myself. I still have no intention of letting AI write for me, but as the underlying technology has continued to level up, every so often I'll run a test to see if it could write a better Techdirt post than I can. I don't think it's there (and I'm still not convinced it will ever get there), but I figured I can share the process with you, and let you be the judge.

sentence: I know that just telling it to write a Techdirt article by itself will lead to pretty bland 'meh' content. So before I even get to the prompt, there are some steps I need to include. First, over time I continue to adjust the underlying 'system prompt' I use for editing my pieces. I won't post the entire system prompt here as it's not that interesting, but I do use it to make it clear its job is to help me be a better writer, not to be a sycophant, not to try to change things just for the sake of change, and to suggest things that will most help the reader.

sentence: Alternative energy policy isn't what it once was in the U.S., but First Solar stock has held up well over the long term, with a 10-year annualized return of 18.5%. The Arizona-based solar power firm is the leading vertically-integrated U.S.-based manufacturer, which has made it an attractive alternative to customers who want to reduce exposure to overseas supply chain disruptions. And First Solar's substantial order backlog continues to show that the business case for solar power -- particularly in an era of oil at $100 a barrel -- continues to ring true regardless of policymakers who ignore the threats of climate change. FSLR is an intriguing growth stock for the coming decade despite near-term policy uncertainty. Revenue is predicted to climb between 15% and 20% in fiscal year 2027, proving this is a stock with staying power regardless of who is setting U.S. energy policy.

sentence: MercadoLibre is perhaps the weakest short-term performer on this list, but it also presents one of the most compelling long-term growth stories in emerging markets. MercadoLibre's growing customer base and expanding logistics network can reinforce its competitive position as more consumers shift their purchases and financial activity online. Shares are down about 20% in the past 12 months, but the long-term revenue growth trends are significant -- including a prediction of 40% expansion in 2026 and another 30% in 2027. With nearly 90 million unique shoppers using its platform, MercadoLibre has the scale necessary to succeed in the long-term. If you're willing to look past recent near-term headwinds, MELI could offer explosive potential growth in the decade to come.

sentence: Highlight: While I got ya, here are nine things and one crazy prediction: 1. Credit where it's due Steve Sarkisian rightfully went on his soapbox last year and chastised the College Football Playoff selection committee for omitting his Texas team from the postseason tournament despite three wins over top-10 teams. And he did it again Monday. Except this time, it was Ohio State he was promoting as a contender, even after the Buckeyes' loss to the Longhorns. "You make the playoffs based off the opinions of others, essentially," he said. "And so that's the risk-reward. I hope Ohio State does not get punished for that game Saturday night. They lost with us scoring with 25 seconds to go in the game. I hope if they end up 9-3, the committee can appreciate the fact that they came to Austin in September, when it was 100 degrees, and played us in that environment. Quite frankly, Ohio State should be rewarded for playing in this game against us. And this isn't crying over spilled milk. But they may go 11-1." Amen. ... Actually, there is some spilled milk, but he's right. Every committee member should give more credit to the Buckeyes than to Indiana, Georgia or Texas Tech, which refused to play stiff nonconference competition. The Hoosiers played Howard or Bill or Tom. ... Speaking of national issues, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), went on "College GameDay" on Saturday to push for passage of the Protect College Sports Act, the bipartisan Senate bill he cosponsored with Washington Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash. Cruz was loudly booed by the crowd, which was made up mostly of UT students. Incidentally, Bo French, the Republican candidate for the Railroad Commission, later shamefully lambasted a diverse section of student fans pictured celebrating because there weren't near enough whites. Or, as he put it, the picture showed that Texas "institutions have been overrun by illegal aliens and foreign nationals." I'm sure he was hoping ICE agents would show up and cart them off so that, in the future, he could see DKR's stands populated only by white, red-meat-eating Texans, resembling those crowds in the '50s. Whites make up less than 32% of the student body, in contrast with Blacks, Asians and Hispanics, who represent up to 59%, and international students, who make up just 4%, according to U.S. News. At least Regents Chairman Kevin Eltife addressed French's racist remarks, saying in a statement: "When I stood on the sidelines at DKR-Texas Memorial Stadium Saturday night and looked up at the seats filled with incredible fans, I saw Longhorns. It's the same remarkable view I have at graduation ceremonies and anytime I'm on campus. I'm proud to celebrate all our Longhorn students today and every day. Thank you for making us proud." ... I do think the Cruz-Cantwell bill would do a lot of good, such as getting rid of the maddening patchwork of state laws, banning college athletes from playing seven or more years and replacing that with a one-time transfer rule, limiting sports agents' commissions to 5% and safeguarding women's and Olympic sports. Those are admirable goals. But the good senator also said the current chaotic system is "terrible for the players." I have yet to hear a single player reject the big NIL checks he's cashing. I haven't heard a single one say he hates having the option to transfer to other schools to better himself and his family financially. Of course, none of these people in charge really care what the athletes think, or they would have invited more--or some--of them to the table to negotiate many of these issues. 2. Manning arrives OK, maybe he wished he hadn't arrived at Monday's press conference because of the insensitive comments he made about an AI-generated fake picture featuring a Sarkisian lookalike slapping Holly Rowe. Nothing about that was funny or decent, and Manning appropriately apologized for being, well, inappropriate. ... It wasn't a flawless performance on the field, either, thanks in large part to five crucial drops by his receivers, which would fluster any quarterback. He even said Monday in his press conference that he felt the effects and "hit a lull" over the next five drives. "I thought I could have responded better." Manning is nothing if not completely accountable. ... But Saturday night was his signature moment, the breakout game that stamped him as a tough-minded leader who never sulks and never stops believing. This was the game even his harshest critics should give him credit for. Was he perfect? Not at all. He still needs more touch on shorter balls. He may never be the most accurate passer because, as Mike Leach always told me, you can't coach accuracy. Ohio State's Julian Sayin is incredibly accurate, but he was 4-for-15 in the second half. ... Arch knew it was going to be a good night when he made it out of the tunnel during the runout for the game. No face-plant amid the eyes-clogging smoke this time, as there was before the Texas State game. He said, "I walked really slowly, and I had my hand on Trevor Goosby." Perfect protection by his left tackle. ... Arch was at his humorous best. He said his uncle Eli texted him, complimenting his patience and his not forcing any passes. When I asked him whether it was harder on him than on his famous uncles because they barely played during the social-media era, Arch objected: "That New York media, that's the real deal." ... Don't question Manning's heart. He's got grit, Sarkisian says. He actually plays better when he's behind. And he gets less help than most because his receivers still drop very catchable passes. Hello, Ryan Wingo. The junior wide receiver has to drastically improve his concentration if he wants a pro career. Texas still needs to throw to Cam Coleman more, and the Auburn transfer also has to improve his hands. ... On Buckeye receiver Jeremiah Smith, Manning said, "He's the real deal." I could see Smith and Miami's Malachi Toney in New York for the Heisman ceremony. ... As for all the blowback on Ryan Day, I wouldn't have let Texas score from the 1-yard line if it meant leaving between 60 and 90 seconds on the clock for Ohio State's offense to have a chance with more time. Have you not paid attention? Ohio State stuffed the Longhorns at the goal line in the Cotton Bowl and in the Horseshoe. Plus, if they had stopped Hollywood Smothers on his leap into the end zone, who knows what Sarkisian would have called after three inefficient runs up the middle? ... I really thought the Buckeyes were gassed in the fourth quarter in the 95-degree heat, especially with the Longhorns stuffing the run. At the suggestion of head football trainer Donald Nguyen, Texas smartly held its pregame warmups in its new indoor facility to save its legs. Every little bit helps.

sentence: I didn't know Bob McKay, who died last week at age 78, well. But I do know he was one of the best offensive linemen in UT history on a level with Jerry Sisemore, Dan Neil, Justin Blalock and Kelvin Banks Jr. And one of the biggest in his era. At 6-5, 236 pounds as a freshman, he was a behemoth and I mean that with the sincerest part of flattery. James Street dubbed him "Big Un" for a reason. ... Student manager Bill Hall said he probably texted McKay every day and remembers him as "one of the nicest human beings. If you were his friend, you were a friend for life." ... Running back teammate Ted Koy remembered McKay as the ultimate competitor on those wishbone days that included a 30-game win streak and two national titles. "If you just followed him," Koy said, "you were going in the right direction." ... McKay came from far, far, far West Texas at Crane, which played in Class AA and which the late Bill Little once wrote had a population of 37 people and 4,700 cattle. Darrell Royal showed up to recruit him, and McKay said, "It was like a parade. Everybody in town wanted to see him." ... Remember, he played on an offensive line that would be considered minuscule these days with teammates on the front like 200-pound Mike Dean. Texas' smallest offensive lineman now is right guard Brandon Baker at a very, uh, light 315 pounds. McKay was coming off shoulder surgery in May 1968. It was the next year that produced Texas' second national championship and was best remembered for the Game of the Century against Arkansas when Street connected with tight end Randy Peschel in one of the biggest pass receptions in school history. The fourth-down throw, which was called 53 Veer Pass, took the Longhorns to the Arkansas 13 and set up the game-winning touchdown and extra point. McKay was the first to reach Peschel downfield and lifted him off the ground, saying, "Nice catch, Pasquale." ... Of course, Texas sealed the national title with a 21-17 win over Notre Dame in the Cotton Bowl on Billy Dale's 1-yard run.

sentence: Had a super time at Imagine Muny 5 at ACL last Thursday night. Good folks are doing everything in their power to preserve one of the most historic municipal golf courses in the country. Scotty Sayers, the longtime manager and friend of Ben Crenshaw, told the audience of about 2,200 that the Muny Conservancy committee is "optimistic" that the University of Texas will agree to keep open the 18-hold course in the heart of downtown that was one of the first golf courses in the South to desegregate and was a breeding ground for Crenshaw, Tom Kite, Mark Brooks and other greats instead of developing the land for commercial purposes. The fifth annual event raised $1 million, auctioning off things like Scottie Scheffler-signed Masters flags, Rory McIlroy-autographed wine bottles and rounds of golf at Pinehurst No. 2 before Ray Benson, Tanya Tucker and Jack Ingram sang. ... Sat with my wife Vicki at a table with Barbara Pruett, a former Texas State Champion, six-time Austin City Golf Champion and legendary instructor at the Barton Creek Golf Academy, and her daughter Paulette. Barbara told me she still plays nine holes every Sunday at Austin Country Club with her 93-year-old dad Roane, a Southwest Conference champion at Texas. Barbara is a Harvey Penick disciple who has taught four generations of Austin golfers. Oh, Paulette told me her five-time city champion father owns a career 22 holes-in-one. sentence: Provost Ed Balleisen announced Wednesday in an email to students new guidelines for using AI tools and platforms in academic work after consulting the Faculty Senate's Educational Policy & Technology Committee, school deans and deans' leadership teams. The Provost Office's updated guidelines build on former Provost Chris Bracey's 2023 guidance, encouraging professors to discuss AI usage with students early in the semester and expanding the scope of the guidelines to include not just AI chatbots but also AI-embedded technologies.

sentence: Bracey's original guidelines - which his office published in April 2023 - highlighted the promise of generative AI tools, encouraging students and faculty to thoughtfully use it in their teaching and research. The guidance provided model language for three tiers of AI policies that professors may choose from. Professors could allow students general permission to use AI in all assignments, only allow them to use AI on specific designated assignments or completely prohibit its usage on all assignments.

sentence: Bracey's guidance states if professors do not list a specific AI policy in their syllabus or discuss one in class, the default rules in the Code of Academic Integrity apply, which state students may not submit content generated, in whole or in part, by AI, and doing so without an instructor's explicit permission constitutes cheating.

Balleisen's model language for professors seeking to provide general permission for AI usage in the classroom also warns students not to simply "cut and paste" large chunks of GAI outputs into their work.

sentence: It comes in 40mm and 44mm sizes. If you don't need a cellular plan, there's a Bluetooth-only Galaxy Watch 9 model. Like the original, the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 comes in a single large 47mm size, with both Bluetooth and LTE baked in by default.  Left to right: Two Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 models, two sizes of the Galaxy Watch 9 (Credit: Eric Zeman)  The Galaxy Watch 9 starts at $379.99 for the Bluetooth-only 40mm model (a $30 price increase compared with the Galaxy Watch 8), while the 44mm model starts at $409.99. Add $50 to either size for the LTE-equipped variant.  The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 costs $699.99, a $50 increase over the original Ultra. That works out to a $320 premium over the base Galaxy Watch 9, or an extra $240 over the most expensive variant (the 44mm Watch 9 with LTE, which costs $459.99).  The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 comes in gray or silver. The 40mm Watch 9 is offered in graphite or cream, and the 44mm version is available in graphite or silver.  Winner: Galaxy Watch 9  Samsung Unveils Two New Galaxy Watches  Power: The Base Model Matches the Ultra  Both the Galaxy Watch 9 and the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 have a new Qualcomm Snapdragon Wear Elite processor that offers better efficiency and increased CPU and GPU performance compared with the Exynos W1000 processor in the Galaxy Watch 8 and the original Ultra. The Ultra 2 has double the storage of the Watch 9, 64GB compared with 32GB, and both have 2GB of memory.  Both watches use Google's Wear OS 7 overlaid with Samsung's One UI 9, each one generation newer than what's currently available on older models, though the Galaxy Watch 8 and original Ultra could get the latest software via an update at some point.  While getting extra storage with the Ultra 2 is a nice bonus, this isn't the reason to spend the extra Benjamins. The Galaxy Watch 9 offers the same power for less.  Winner: Tie  Battery Life: The Main Reason to Pay More  The Ultra 2 has more battery capacity and lasts much longer than the Watch 9 between charges, and that's the main reason to spend more for the premium model if you're not into adventuring.  Specifically, the Ultra 2 has an 800mAh cell and an estimated battery life of 60 hours on a charge with the always-on display enabled. That's a sizable increase over the original Ultra, which has a 590mAh battery with an estimated 48 hours of power per charge. In testing, the Ultra 2 outlasted the company's estimate, running for an impressive 69.5 hours under normal use with the always-on display enabled, up from 46 hours for the original Ultra.  The Galaxy Watch 9 only lasts a day between charges (Credit: Joseph Maldonado)  Both Galaxy Watch 9 sizes have much smaller cells than the Ultra 2; the 40mm has 390mAh, while the 44mm has 445mAh. Both figures are larger than their respective Watch 8 counterparts (325mAh for the 40mm and 435mAh for the 44mm), but the Watch 9 has the same 30-hour battery estimate as its predecessor. Both the Watch 9 and the Watch 8 lasted for 26 hours on a charge in testing, slightly undercutting Samsung's estimate.  Battery has been a weak spot for Samsung's flagship smartwatches for years. Despite its more efficient chip and increased battery capacity compared with the last generation, the Galaxy Watch 9 doesn't offer improved battery life. On the other hand, the Ultra 2 offers a significant improvement over its predecessor, and lasts almost two full days more than the mainline Galaxy Watch 9.  Winner: Galaxy Watch Ultra 2  Screen: 5,000 Nits of Overkill?  The Galaxy Watch 9 screen matches the size and specs of its predecessor. The 44mm model has a 1.5-inch, 480-by-480-pixel Super AMOLED screen, while the 40mm version has a 1.3-inch, 432-by-432-pixel display. Regardless of size, the screen tops out at 3,000 nits of brightness, which is more than bright enough to see in direct sunlight.  The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2's screen can reach 5,000 nits of brightness (Credit: Eric Zeman)  The Ultra 2 has a 1.52-inch, 498-by-498-pixel Super AMOLED screen, which is larger and higher-res than the 44mm Watch 9, and the original Ultra (1.5 inches, 480 by 480 pixels). The screen reaches a blinding 5,000 nits, up from 3,000 nits in the original Ultra. While the figure is impressive, it doesn't significantly improve readability, since 3,000 nits is already more than sufficient for most lighting conditions. That said, I appreciate the bump when looking at the screen in direct sunlight or using the watch as a flashlight.  Winner: Galaxy Watch Ultra 2  Design and Durability: Only One Can Handle Scuba Descents  Both the Galaxy Watch 9 and the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 have a squircle shape that the company first introduced with the original Galaxy Watch Ultra. The squared bezel and circular watch face sit above a dynamic lug system meant to keep the sensors in close contact with your skin as you move throughout the day. Samsung calls it a cushion design.  Both watches come with redesigned, lighter bands that feature air pockets for improved ventilation. Aside from the bands, the Ultra 2 is lighter than its predecessor, and the case is still made from durable titanium, whereas the Watch 9 is encased in aluminum.  The Galxy Watch Ultra 2 has more buttons than the Galaxy Watch 9 (Credit: Eric Zeman)  The Ultra 2 is also much more durable than its less expensive sibling, and this added ruggedness is the main reason to consider spending up for it. That said, the Galaxy Watch 9 is no slouch when it comes to durability. An IP68 rating ensures the Galaxy Watch 9 is impervious to dust and can be submerged in water, while its 5ATM rating means it can withstand underwater depths of up to 164 feet (50 meters). The Watch 9 even has a MIL-STD-810H rating, a military durability standard, meaning it can withstand extreme temperature changes, blowing sand, and other environmental stressors, such as vibration and shock.  The Ultra 2 offers a superior 10ATM rating, meaning it can be submerged to depths of 328 feet (100 meters), an IP69K resistance rating ensuring protection from high-pressure water jets, and the same military endurance certification as the Watch 9. On top of that, the Ultra 2 carries an EN13319 diving certification, whereas the original Ultra and the Galaxy Watch 9 are not safe for scuba descents. Overall, the Ultra 2 is well-suited for rough-and-tumble adventures on land or at sea.  Winner: Galaxy Watch Ultra 2  Recommended by Our Editors  Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 vs. Watch 8: Should You Upgrade?  Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 vs. Apple Watch Ultra 3: Which Is the Best Adventure Companion?  The Best Smartwatches for 2026  Fitness and Health: Niche Outdoor Tools vs. Everyday Metrics  The Galaxy Watch 9 and the Ultra 2 debut with a handful of new health features, including a Heart Health Score that monitors your overnight blood pressure and daily activity to assess your risk of heart disease, and provides tips to improve the score. Fitness Index quantifies your well-being, showing body composition, cardio, endurance, flexibility, and strength in a single spider chart. Daily Cardio Load gives runners an idea of how much to push in a day to maximize gains without burnout.  Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 (Credit: Eric Zeman)  The latest Galaxy Watches also monitor your vitals. After establishing baseline values for your blood oxygen saturation, heart rate, heart rate variability, respiratory rate, and skin temperature, they notify you of any concerning deviations they notice.  To support your adventures, the Ultra 2 comes with a couple of unique features to keep you informed as you hike or dive. Trail Run monitors your elevation and route, and tracks your terrain to warn you if it's rough enough to cause potential injury. A Nutrition Alert tracks your sweat loss and reminds you to hydrate. In the water, the Diving app can track depth and temperature as well as safe ascent and descent speeds.  These new features join the Galaxy Watch line's already impressive list of health and wellness capabilities. An AI coach provides guidance on running and sleeping. Overnight, the Galaxy Watch can listen for snoring (when paired with a nearby Samsung phone) and monitor for sleep apnea. You can also use the watch to check your body composition, similar to a smart scale. An antioxidant test provides insight into your diet, vascular load detection checks your arterial health, and advanced glycation end products (AGEs) index tracking provides a detailed picture of your metabolism.  In testing, both proved to be accurate exercise trackers but showed occasional gaps in the sleep data they collected, skewing the otherwise precise numbers.  Winner: Galaxy Watch Ultra 2  Lifestyle Features: Why You Don't Need the Ultra for AI  Both the Galaxy Watch 9 and the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 have access to many useful third-party Wear OS apps, including Google's many tools and popular options like Spotify and Strava. Both have Google's Gemini built in to answer questions, send texts, and interact with Samsung apps such as Calendar, Clock, Health, and Reminder via voice commands. sentence: Foreign and impassable to humans who can only dream of what lies below the water, the depths of Earth's oceans are a place of mystery. Composer Lei Liang and oceanographer Joshua Jones, two UC San Diego researchers intrigued by the immeasurable seas, sought to demystify them through sound. Their pursuits culminated in "The Inaudible Ocean," a sold-out collaborative chamber music event between Liang, Jones, and Liang's Lei Lab, which premiered at the Conrad Prebys Concert Hall on May 20.

filename: P4-027__'The Inaudible Ocean' delivers on its premise - perhaps too well - The UCSD Guardian.txt
sentence: Fascinated by the elusive soundscapes of the underwater realm and its diverse populace, Liang and Jones brought sounds beyond human hearing into concert. They presented dynamic whale songs, dolphin clicks, and even the groaning of ice floes in concert -- all sounds that are usually well outside the 20 hertz to 20,000 hertz range of human hearing. Whales, for example, can produce sound that is both infrasonic - as low as 10 hertz - and ultrasonic - up to 150,000 hertz. This task captured me from the get-go, and I sat down in the packed concert hall excited and curious about how Liang and Jones would translate the noises of the ocean into music.

sentence: Contrabassist Mark Dresser, percussionist Steven Schick, and pianist Cory Smythe performed the hourlong event, which was broken into seven movements all backed by real underwater recordings of ocean life captured all over the globe. The lighting and staging were both simple, drawing focus to the three musicians onstage. Each subsequent movement incorporated these audio recordings at a decelerated rate to make their nuances easier to hear over time. Dresser, Schick, and Smyth - incredibly talented musicians and longtime affiliates of UCSD's music department - used their instruments in unconventional ways. They played below the contrabass' bridge, modulated piano strings to intentionally sound off tune, and mimicked the percussive cetacean calls by tapping on the rivets, screws, and rims of their wooden and metallic bodies.

sentence: As a longtime concertgoer across many genres and cultures, "The Inaudible Ocean" was one of the most experimental works I have seen to date. However, this degree of experimentation felt too avant-garde; each movement lasted for almost 10 minutes, with little melody to follow. To an ear untrained on the subtleties between whale species, the movements sounded similar to one another despite the progressively slowed-down background audio. These sentiments resonated with most of the audience that night, as palpable confusion rippled throughout the concert hall when the show ended. Since this was my first exposure to Liang and his lab's work, I was unacquainted with the ambient nature of his repertoire. Without knowing his prior projects - which heavily focus on sound design and the Lei Lab's audio research - I admittedly had my expectations set for something more traditional.

sentence: It was visually interesting to watch highly skilled professionals challenge what sounds could be produced by orthodox Western instruments, but the night seemed to linger longer on reconstructing underwater noises rather than creating melodic arrangements. These sparse moments when the instruments sang were definitely the performance's highlights, and I wished the concept had leaned further in this direction. It could be argued that Liang and Jones' vision was realized too literally. Despite the undeniable technical achievement of this effort, for me, "The Inaudible Ocean" is a musical project I would have preferred to have included more music.

sentence: Searching the web usually requires you to stop what you are doing, open a tab, and actively look for updates. Well, a major tech giant wants to change that dynamic entirely. Following its initial tease at I/O 2026, Google has officially started rolling out 'Search agents' in its AI Mode. The upgrade turns the traditional search engine into a proactive assistant that works quietly in the background.

sentence: Instead of waiting for you to type a query, these new information agents run 24/7. The goal is to catch relevant changes the moment they happen.

sentence: Setting one up is relatively straightforward. In AI Mode, users can simply type phrases like 'keep me updated on' or 'alert me when' followed by their specific criteria. For instance, they could instruct the agent to track local real estate listings that match your exact budget and square footage requirements. They could also ask it to monitor when a specific athlete drops a new sneaker collaboration. Once the agent finds a match, it delivers a synthesized update and offers quick actions to follow up (via 9to5Google).

sentence: Canva is an all-in-one bundle for everyday creators: a browser-first suite that makes it easy to design social posts, presentations, simple videos, print materials, and brand kits without needing pro expertise. For a while, Canva was "enough" for 90% of what people make, and anything heavier-like advanced photo compositing, full motion graphics pipelines, high-end audio-usually lived elsewhere. sentence: Artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated in our daily lives, or at least it appears that way on our social media feeds. sentence: First, the economic tradeoffs. The building of data centers means construction jobs. It can also mean substantial increases in property tax revenue, which could help fund city services. For example, Loudoun County, Virginia, which has the highest concentration of data centers in the country, gets 38% of its revenue from the centers every year. However, these warehouse-sized buildings   some the size of multiple football fields   take up valuable land that could be used for other purposes, such as much-needed housing or commercial development that provides permanent jobs.

sentence: Then there are the environmental tradeoffs. It has been reported that one data center can use as much electricity annually as 200,000 homes. Three facilities could consume double that of the city of Seattle. This is hard to square as Anchorage and state policymakers contemplate an impending natural gas shortage and other utility issues. Data centers also require a large amount of water for cooling the heat-emitting electronics they house. Public records from Memphis have shown a data center there using 11 million gallons in one month, nearly equivalent to what 150 homes use in an entire year.

sentence: What does this new code update do? Importantly, it does not outright ban or prohibit data centers. First, it adds a definition to our code of what data centers are. Second, it clarifies which zoning will allow data centers and makes data centers adhere to conditional use permitting. Simply put, this means data centers won't be built in neighborhoods and will involve more municipal oversight and public process if a project is proposed. Additionally, our ordinance requires 200-foot setbacks, visual screening and landscaping, fire suppression, noise mitigation studies, and documentation of power generation and storage.

sentence: As Donald Trump engages in the bold midterm election strategy of telling 75 percent of the country that they will be “backwards and poor” if they refuse to allow substantial portions of land to be handed over to data centers, he’s one expression of transpartisan outrage behind. Anger is building just as persistently about Flock cameras, the automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) powered by artificial intelligence and the data centers that make AI run, which are used increasingly by law enforcement to surveil and track citizens, often improperly.

sentence: People are as concerned about the panopticon of ever-present surveillance as they are about the implications of an artificial intelligence sold to the public as destroying jobs if not the planet. But the two technology rollouts share something else in common: the rather sneaky ways in which they are being foisted on the public.

sentence: City officials repeatedly are signing nondisclosure agreements with developers and concealing the details about data center development from the public. Flock cameras have also appeared without public deliberation or warning in a lot of communities, but the bigger issue is that municipalities are purchasing the equipment with money originally intended for other purposes.

sentence: In both cases, the secrecy and underhandedness give the impression that public officials value tech partnerships more than transparency, and that there really is something to hide with these systems. People clearly want a voice in deciding the future of their communities and the terms upon which that future will proceed. In this sense, data centers and Flock cameras are in some ways physical manifestations of the nation’s soaring inequality, an egregious example of how economic power gets translated into political power. Shady closed-door deals just make that perception more egregious.

sentence: Diverting settlement funds for other uses is a favorite pastime of the powerful. In the aftermath of the foreclosure fraud settlement, states stole the money to fill budget holes or other purposes rather than help victims of illegal foreclosures. The latest pot of cash that states can raid comes from the national opioid settlement. More than $50 billion was made available to heal communities destroyed by the epidemic, expected to be spent on initiatives like treatment and detox centers and anti-overdose medications.

sentence: But as a KFF investigation reveals, a nontrivial amount of these settlement funds has gone into policing for things like Tasers and drones. And since law enforcement loves nothing more than purchasing new toys, that also means that opioid settlement dollars are buying Flock cameras. Mother Jones was able to find 19 agencies in ten states that have spent close to $1 million on ALPRs; the total number is likely much higher.

sentence: Police departments have justified this by saying that ALPRs can fight crime, and drug crime in particular, and therefore will prevent epidemics from recurring. But that is manifestly not the purpose of the opioid settlement, which was to get help for addicted people who needed it. Incredibly, seven of the 19 expenditures on ALPRs came out of West Virginia, ground zero of the opioid crisis.

sentence: That may not be the most outrageous Flock financing scheme. In Texas, the legislature imposed a new $1 fee on auto insurance, they said to combat the persistent stealing of catalytic converters, which is real (says this victim of catalytic converter theft). But $30 million in revenues from that fee (out of a total of $81 million) has been diverted toward purchasing and installing Flock cameras along state highways, according to The Texas Tribune. That’s 3,200 Flock cameras coming from the auto insurance fee.

sentence: It's not necessarily the tech itself that's to blame either, though reports say certain workers feel distinct unease about being forced to use AI systems. For example, one consultant argued that AI's arrival is driving a near-constant sense of urgency in delivering work that can emphasize any feelings of psychological unsafety, leading to burnout. This parallels numerous reports of company leadership rolling out AI without adding in necessary training, then expecting workers to just deliver boosted productivity. sentence: Economic policy has lately been convulsed by a proposition unthinkable under past Republican administrations: increased public ownership of major stakes in private companies. Under a growing array of public-equity deals engineered by the Trump White House, US government agencies are going well beyond their former arm's-length initiatives to influence corporate decision-making to become shareholders in the companies themselves.
title: How Public Equity Can Promote a Revived American Democracy

sentence: This move is stoking ideological blowback. The  laissez-faire right sees it undermining the traditional divide between the market (good) and the state (bad). Adam Kinzinger and Joe Scarborough- Republicans of the Never Trump persuasion-have derided the policy as ' ACTUAL communism/socialism' and called for privatizing the Trump equity stakes. Even left economist Robert Reich, whom the Cato Institute once attacked for advocating industrial policy, has now outflanked Cato by likening Trump's taking of equity stakes to Nazism.

sentence: All this inflammatory rhetoric serves mostly to distract attention from the real policy questions at the heart of the public-equity debate, which are at their core about democracy. As technologies like AI boom, will the public get any meaningful say in how a handful of companies remake the American workplace, public discourse, and much of our common world?
title: How Public Equity Can Promote a Revived American Democracy

sentence: Part of the problem with the Trump administration's abrupt lurch into equity ownership last year is that public debate has played little or no role. As Trump regulators in the Commerce Department retired a Biden-era grant to semiconductor maker Intel, they demanded a 10 percent equity stake in the company itself-a position that is now worth  five times more than the government paid for it. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick did not make much attempt to justify the move, other than to issue decidedly nonideological and pragmatic comments about national security, and a better return for the American taxpayer than what was realized under the Biden approach of 'just giving grants away.'
title: How Public Equity Can Promote a Revived American Democracy

sentence: It turns out that was just the beginning of the Trump public-equity binge. Despite having almost no support from more traditional Republicans, the administration kept plowing ahead, announcing  shareholding deals with more than two dozen companies worth billions of dollars, in sectors ranging from rare earths to energy.

sentence: Despite the unease from some quarters here at home, other major economies around the world have not been shy in pursuing their national interest by holding public-equity stakes in private companies and maintaining sovereign wealth funds to manage them. China is the extreme example of a state capitalism that involves government closely in the means of production-but  virtually every other country in Europe and Asia has adopted a 'lite' version of the same practice. Iconic firms from Volkswagen to Renault to British Steel are owned in part or fully by public agencies, limiting the offshoring of jobs and better aligning corporate practices with the national interest.

sentence: Equity stakes can also potentially solve a problem that bedeviled economic officials in the Biden administration: speed. Traditional government tools such grants, loans, and antitrust legal actions can take years to negotiate or litigate, while markets move in hours and days. Look at the experience of the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund under Biden, intended to further solar and other projects. It  took two years after the Inflation Reduction Act authorized the office for the grants to be obligated-and even then, the recipients did not have the funds on hand when Trump came back into office. He quickly killed the program. In contrast, equity deals can be inked at the speed of corporate transactions. Within months of acquiring partial control over US Steel, the Trump administration forced the company to reopen a Granite City, Illinois, facility staffed by unionized steelworkers.

sentence: That's the thinking behind Bernie Sanders's proposal for an American AI Sovereign Wealth Fund. While Sanders's fund bears a superficial resemblance to the earlier Trump public-equity deals, it's much more ambitious and far-reaching than they are. Sanders proposes to mandate that any AI company earning more than $200 million make a  one-time deposit of 50 percent of its shares in a publicly owned sovereign wealth fund. California Governor Gavin Newsom embraced a version of the idea, as did Sam Altman of OpenAI and Michigan Democratic Senate hopeful Abdul el-Sayed.
title: How Public Equity Can Promote a Revived American Democracy

sentence: Sanders's plan, and the follow-up proposals it sparked, reverses the traditional model of equity partnerships: The dominant capital flow here comes not from government to a corporation in the first instance but from a corporation to government, via a gift of shares to the Treasury. It would thus substantially lower tech billionaires' net worth.

sentence: These ideas could have significant revenue implications. Sanders estimates that the transfer could represent $7 trillion in value to the federal government. That's a number almost equivalent to the entire  federal US budget in 2025, and more than three times the size of Norway's sovereign wealth fund (currently the world's largest). This could go a long way toward helping any workers displaced by AI to get back on their feet, or addressing the climate crisis, which could be set back by the runaway erection of gas-fueled AI data centers.

sentence: But money is only part of the reason to take equity stakes-and a fairly small part at that. After all, it is entirely possible that AI is a bubble  that will pop, rendering a massive tranche of government-held shares comparatively worthless. Even without a full-on meltdown in the AI sector, the actual cash flow value to the US government isn't rooted in the paper value of the shares it might sell but the annual dividends they bring while the government holds onto them. Even at current valuations, that's only likely to be in the tens of billions-not that much in the grand scheme of federal budgeting.

sentence: The bigger reason to seriously consider some version of Sanders's sovereign wealth fund is to shore up our beleaguered democracy. Equity stakes empower the government to use shareholder votes and even occupy board seats. That, in turn, allows public officials to help steer corporate policy from the inside, or as the writer Matt Bruenig puts it, to exert ' more fine-tuned control' over consequential economic decisions.

sentence: Markets aggregate consumer preferences through purchases, but with equity stakes and sovereign wealth funds, we can aggregate citizen preferences about how a general-purpose technology should be governed. A public equity stake, if designed with real anti-corruption guardrails, is one of the few tools that can help achieve these critical aims.

sentence: Public ownership can also help meet the challenges already emerging in the AI sector: If management is pushing coders to pump out exploitative and misleading AI slop in the name of short-term profits, a public voice on a corporate board can rescind that policy directive on pain of dismissal. If data centers rely on emissions-intensive natural gas rather than renewable energy sources, a vote from a company board can set them straight.

sentence: These are not hypothetical thought experiments. Norway's sovereign wealth fund uses its shares to limit executive compensation,  have employees represented on boards, and promote the hiring of women. France's fund votes its shares to push for greater climate disclosure; Singapore's fund promotes corporate alignment with ESG targets. And the Norwegian government has instructed its own fund to push all the companies in its vast 7,000-plus-company portfolio to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050-even though the initial source of this wealth is Norway's fossil-fuel production. This offers a precedent for how government guardrails can tilt against the profit motive of a constituent industry, and how social movements can leverage these commitments to hold the fund's feet to the fire.

sentence: None of this is to suggest that public-equity stakes are a panacea. There are plenty of reasons to believe the actually existing US government would fail to use equity stakes in the public interest. A centrist government might dogmatically refrain from going against company management; a MAGA government might push boards to help the president's family enrich itself or oppose sustainability standards (this latter mandate is indeed now encoded in  a bill before the Alaskan legislature as it seeks to direct the priorities of the state's sovereign wealth fund). Moreover, the entanglement of private and public interest might further advance the rampant corruption we see in our political and economic life, provoking private interests to further intervene in our elections, or public officials to be still more deeply aligned with and captured by the interests of that of capital.
title: How Public Equity Can Promote a Revived American Democracy

sentence: But these problems can be addressed. Congress has to step up and exercise oversight and control over government shareholding votes in the same way that it does over regulatory actions, to ensure that the public's representatives at companies exercise independence from management. On the politics side, this tsunami of private electioneering is happening  even without public-equity stakes-a strong indication that campaign finance and court reform are the way to tackle the problem at its source. And any pro-democracy movement worth its salt has to recognize strong public opportunities where they emerge. This year has seen an explosion of activism against data centers, and primary election upsets against candidates backed by AI donors. Public-equity stakes allow parties and movements to lay out a vision for how they would use influence over the AI industry and to specify what guardrails may be necessary to make that influence resistant to corruption of all kinds.
title: How Public Equity Can Promote a Revived American Democracy

filename: P4-065__How Public Equity Can Promote a Revived American Democracy.txt
sentence: Some critics suggest that it's better to wait for a more ideologically sensible government to take office before embracing a broad vision of public-equity stakes and sovereign wealth funds to advance small-d democracy in our billionaire-blighted political economy. But given the speed of technological and political development, our current democratic emergency may not afford us that luxury. What's more, there are precedents for taking inadequate proposals by right-wing administrations and making them better in the future. America's most ambitious program to advance public equity-the 1932-57  Reconstruction Finance Corporation (RFC)-was created in the waning days of the Hoover administration to administer a patchwork system of economic relief in the early days of the Great Depression. During the New Deal, Franklin Delano Roosevelt's administration turbocharged the RFC to build housing, infrastructure, energy, and war-preparedness projects. Today's conditions are similar: The companies Trump has invested in are aware that future administrations could well adopt a different agenda that they will have to adapt to, and they've said as much in their security filings.
title: How Public Equity Can Promote a Revived American Democracy

sentence: In the face of the Depression, FDR and his allies recognized the need to act boldly and creatively to reassert public influence over the direction of the American political economy. The interlocking crisis of democracy, MAGA authoritarianism, and unchecked AI impunity demand that we act in the same fashion-and leaders like Sanders, Newsom, and el-Sayed are pointing to the path forward.
